title: The Velvet Gentleman: Honfleur, the Butte, and the Room in Arcueil Nobody Entered
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: Honfleur, the House by the Harbor

stops.name: Honfleur, birth on the boulevard Charles V
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day
stops.campa: In three linked half-timbered houses a few streets above the harbor, Alfred Satie, shipping broker, and Jane Leslie Anton, of Scottish Protestant family, have a son. They register him Eric Alfred Leslie and baptize him Anglican. Honfleur is a working port on the Seine estuary, its light already pulling painters down from Paris. Olga follows in 1867, Conrad in 1869. The house outlives everyone born in it: in 1998 it opens as a museum of the boy, with a mechanical winged pear and a piano that plays itself.
stops.quote: I came into the world very young in an age that was very old.
stops.quote_source: Erik Satie, inscription accompanying his own self-portrait caricature, via Wikiquote
suggested_refs: Les Maisons Satie, 67 boulevard Charles V, Honfleur, the birth house

stops.name: Honfleur, the swimming lesson at the Vieux Bassin
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: family anecdote, undated in every telling, placed c. 1868-1870; month and day defaulted
stops.campa: At the Vieux Bassin, where the tall narrow houses stand with their feet in the water, an uncle named Adrien takes the small boy out for a swimming lesson. Honfleur calls this uncle the sea bird: he keeps a boat he does not sail and a box at the theatre he does not fill. The lesson goes wrong and the child nearly drowns. The family keeps the story and no document behind it survives. Every teller since has repeated it undated, and it is the earliest thing anyone claims to know about him.
suggested_refs: The Vieux Bassin of Honfleur, painted by Boudin and Jongkind in these same years
sources: Ornella Volta, Satie biographical tradition, via the atlas geography lens (not independently verified)

stops.name: Paris, the family moves after the war
stops.date_confidence: attested as following the Franco-Prussian War, which ends May 1871; the pool's geography lens wrongly gave 1870 and the war's outbreak; month and day unrecorded and defaulted
stops.campa: The war with Prussia ends. Alfred Satie sells the brokerage at Honfleur and takes the household to Paris, where he finds work as a translator. They are provincials in the capital and they are not rich. Erik is five. No reachable source records the street or the number, so this stop stands on the centroid of the city rather than on a doorway. The arrangement lasts barely a year, and what ends it is his mother's death. Paris will take the boy back and give him up twice more before he is twenty.
suggested_refs: Alfred Satie's Paris translation work, 1871-1878, address unrecorded

stops.name: Honfleur, the second baptism
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; day and parish unrecorded in any reachable source
stops.campa: Jane Leslie Satie dies in Paris. Erik and Conrad are put on a train back to Normandy and handed to their father's parents; Olga goes elsewhere. The grandparents are Catholic and the boys were baptized Anglican, so the boys are baptized a second time, at six years old and at three. Satie will spend his life founding churches, joining them and quitting them: Péladan's Rose+Croix, then a metropolitan church of art with one member, himself. None of them is the church he was given twice before he could object.
suggested_refs: The paternal grandparents' house at Honfleur, where Satie was raised 1872-1878

stops.name: Honfleur, lessons with the organist Vinot
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; Vinot's church is not named in any reachable source, so the pin follows the grandparents' house
stops.campa: The grandmother sends the boy to Gustave Vinot, organist of the town, and Satie begins the only musical training he will never resent. Vinot teaches plainchant and the older church modes, the music of a Normandy port rather than the salon repertoire of the capital. The Gymnopédies and the Gnossiennes, twenty years off, run on bare parallel chords and decline to resolve. The modes are the ones from the choir loft, and they predate the harmony the Conservatoire will shortly try to teach him.
suggested_refs: Gustave Vinot, organist at Honfleur, Satie's first teacher; his church is unidentified

stops.name: Paris, sent back to the father
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; the pool's geography lens wrongly compressed this with the father's remarriage, which en.wikipedia dates to January 1879
stops.campa: The grandmother dies and the boy of twelve is put on the train the other way, back to his father in Paris. The remarriage comes after him: in January 1879 Alfred Satie marries Eugénie Barnetche, a pianist and composer of salon pieces, who takes an interest in the stepson's musical future and arranges for him to be examined. Satie will remember the house as a place to be escaped from, and will one day enlist in the infantry rather than remain in it.
suggested_refs: Eugénie Barnetche, pianist and composer, Satie's stepmother from January 1879

stops.name: Paris, the preparatory piano class at the Conservatoire
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month
stops.campa: At thirteen he enters the Conservatoire on the rue du Conservatoire, in the preparatory piano class, and dislikes it inside a week. He will describe the building afterwards without softening anything, as a district prison with no beauty inside or out. The institution returns the judgement in full. His stepmother had arranged the examination that got him in. He plays badly on purpose and well by accident, and reads what he is not assigned. He stays three years.
stops.quote: a vast, very uncomfortable, and rather ugly building; a sort of district prison with no beauty on the inside, nor on the outside, for that matter
stops.quote_source: Erik Satie on the Paris Conservatoire, quoted in Wikipedia, 'Erik Satie'
suggested_refs: The Conservatoire de Paris on the rue du Conservatoire, 9th arrondissement

stops.name: Paris, the laziest student and the expulsion
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year for the remark; the pool's quote lens misdated it to 1880. Expulsion follows in 1882
stops.campa: Émile Decombes, his piano teacher, sets down the verdict that will be quoted for a century. The following year the institution acts on it and Satie is dismissed for unsatisfactory performance. He is sixteen. He comes back in 1885 to the intermediate class, is judged worthless a second time, and leaves again without a diploma of any kind. The Schola Cantorum will finally give him one twenty-seven years later, when he is forty-two and has walked in and asked for it himself.
stops.quote: the laziest student in the Conservatoire
stops.quote_source: Émile Decombes, Satie's piano teacher, 1881, quoted in Wikipedia, 'Erik Satie'
suggested_refs: Émile Decombes, piano teacher at the Conservatoire, and his report on the young Satie

stops.name: Honfleur, the Allegro signed Erik
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; the pool's chronology lens wrongly placed the composition in Paris, en.wikipedia gives Honfleur
stops.campa: Back at Honfleur between failures, the eighteen-year-old writes a short Allegro for piano, the first composition of his that survives, and signs it with a spelling his baptismal record does not contain. Eric becomes Erik, the Norse form, a name off the sea coast rather than out of the parish register. Nothing in the piece announces anything. The signature does. From this sheet forward, every score, pamphlet and insult he issues carries the invented k.
suggested_refs: The Allegro of 1884, Satie's first surviving composition and first use of 'Erik'

stops.name: Paris, readmitted to the intermediate class
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; month unrecorded and defaulted
stops.campa: He is taken back into the Conservatoire, into the intermediate piano class, and the second attempt goes the way of the first. The teachers find nothing in him and he finds nothing in them worth taking. He leaves with no certificate and with the standing of a young man the profession has examined twice and declined twice. What he carries out of the building is a grievance against trained musicians, and he takes it up the hill to Montmartre, where nobody is asked for papers.
suggested_refs: Satie's second Conservatoire enrolment, 1885, ended without a diploma

stops.name: Arras, the 33rd Infantry Regiment
stops.date_confidence: enlistment attested to November 1886; the deliberate bronchitis is reconstruction, called standard biographical tradition by the pool's own geography lens
stops.campa: Rather than stay in his father's house he volunteers for the 33rd Infantry Regiment, garrisoned at Arras in the north, and finds within weeks that a barracks is a Conservatoire with worse food. The tradition holds that he engineered his own release, baring his chest to the winter air until the bronchitis arrived and then coughing his way out through the infirmary. The regiment invalids him out in 1887. The lung complaint stays with him. He does not set foot in another institution until 1905, when he walks into one and asks to be taught.
suggested_refs: The 33rd Infantry Regiment barracks at Arras

stops.name: Montmartre, the room on the lower slope
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; month unrecorded and defaulted
stops.campa: Discharged, he takes a room in the ninth arrondissement at the foot of the Butte and joins the population of the hill, the painters and poets who do not sell and the cabaret singers who feed them after dark. The Ogives, four pieces built out of plainchant of the kind Vinot taught him at Honfleur, are already written. He is twenty-one, has no diploma and no income, and is living for the first time in the one quarter of Paris that will ask him for neither.
suggested_refs: The Ogives, conventionally dated 1886, before the Montmartre move

stops.name: Montmartre, second pianist at the Chat Noir
stops.date_confidence: attested to the period 1887-1888; month unrecorded, set mid-year to hold travel order
stops.campa: At 12 rue Victor-Massé, Rodolphe Salis runs the Chat Noir, and Satie becomes first a fixture and then its second pianist, playing behind shadow plays and drunken recitations for a wage that barely covers the room. Here he meets Contamine de Latour, the poet who will supply him with texts and with nicknames, and learns the trade he will practise for thirty years: music written to be walked past. Rudolf Laban will draw posters for the revues of this same hill by night, a dozen years after.
suggested_refs: Le Chat Noir at 12 rue Victor-Massé, Salis's second premises

stops.name: Montmartre, the Gymnopedies and the Gnossiennes
stops.date_confidence: Gymnopédies attested to 1888, Gnossiennes to 1889; months unrecorded and defaulted
stops.campa: In a lodging on the Butte he writes three slow pieces in three-four time and calls them Gymnopédies, after the naked dances of Spartan boys. The next year come the first Gnossiennes, without bar lines, with instructions to the player set where the tempo marks belong. Nobody buys them. He is twenty-two and is playing cabaret at night to pay for the lodging. A few streets off, in the Cimetière de Montmartre, François Delsarte has lain since 1871; Falconetti's ashes will be laid there in 1960.
suggested_refs: The three Gymnopédies (1888) and the first Gnossiennes (1889)

stops.name: Montmartre, meeting Debussy at the Auberge du Clou
stops.date_confidence: contested: the pool's chronology lens gives 1890, its geography lens 1891, and en.wikipedia names the venue with no year. 1891 followed as conventional; month unrecorded and defaulted
stops.campa: At the Auberge du Clou on the avenue Trudaine, where he has taken a second pianist's post, Satie meets Claude Debussy. They are within four years of the same age and equally unplaced. The friendship runs a quarter of a century and is never comfortable: Debussy orchestrates two of the Gymnopédies and makes them famous, and Satie watches the world hand his friend the reception it withholds from him. In 1917 the resentment finally speaks and the two part. Debussy dies the following March.
suggested_refs: The Auberge du Clou, avenue Trudaine, where Satie and Debussy met
sources: Robert Orledge, Satie the Composer, and Ornella Volta, via the atlas geography lens (venue not independently re-fetched)

segments.name: The Rose+Croix and the Church of One

stops.name: Paris, the Salon de la Rose+Croix at the Galerie Durand-Ruel
stops.date_confidence: the first Salon opens March 1892, attested; Satie's appointment as the order's composer is dated 1890 by the pool's chronology lens and 1891 by fr.wikipedia, unresolved
stops.campa: Joséphin Péladan, who styles himself Sâr and revives the Rosicrucians as an order of Catholic art, makes Satie composer to the Ordre de la Rose-Croix. At the Galerie Durand-Ruel on the rue Laffitte the first Salon opens with his fanfares in the air and Symbolist canvases on the walls. It runs for months. By the middle of the year Satie has broken with Péladan over Uspud and declared himself the only true composer of the order, which now has one member and no premises.
suggested_refs: The first Salon de la Rose+Croix, Galerie Durand-Ruel, March 1892
sources: Robert Orledge, Satie the Composer, via the atlas geography lens

stops.name: Montmartre, five months with Suzanne Valadon
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1893, a liaison of five months; the pool's geography lens wrongly gave 1893-1896. Month unrecorded and defaulted
stops.campa: The painter Suzanne Valadon takes the room next to his on the rue Cortot. He proposes marriage after the first night. She refuses and stays five months, and in those months he writes the Danses gothiques, which he calls a novena for the peace of his soul. Then she leaves. It is the only romantic attachment recorded in his life. He is twenty-seven, with thirty-two years still to run, and the biographies that call him a solitary are counting from this landing.
suggested_refs: 6 rue Cortot, Montmartre, the Satie and Valadon rooms

stops.name: Montmartre, the Metropolitan Church of Art of Jesus the Conductor
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; month unrecorded, set mid-year to hold travel order
stops.campa: He founds a church. Its name is the Église Métropolitaine d'Art de Jésus Conducteur, its congregation is one man, and its sole officer, Parcier et Maître de Chapelle, is the same man. From the Abbatiale, which is his rented room, he issues bulls against critics, conductors and rival composers, correctly formatted, properly sealed and posted. Twenty-four years later a court will fine him for a postcard. The habit of writing insults on paper with his name at the bottom is already fixed.
suggested_refs: The Cartulaire de l'Église Métropolitaine d'Art de Jésus Conducteur, Satie's one-man bulletin

stops.name: Montmartre, the 840 repetitions of Vexations
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the manuscript is undated and carries no year; scholars assign c. 1893-1894 on musical and biographical grounds. Month set to hold travel order
stops.campa: On a single undated sheet he writes a short bass line, harmonizes it twice, and adds a note in the margin about playing the motif eight hundred and forty times in succession and preparing beforehand in the deepest silence. He neither performs it nor publishes it. The sheet goes into the room with everything else. Seventy years later John Cage will take the instruction literally, and the piece will run more than eighteen hours in a theatre on Third Avenue in Manhattan.
stops.quote: prepare himself, in the deepest silence, by serious immobilities
stops.quote_source: Erik Satie, preface to Vexations, quoted in French Wikipedia, 'Erik Satie'
suggested_refs: The undated autograph of Vexations, with its performance note

stops.name: Paris, seven velvet suits
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; month unrecorded and defaulted
stops.campa: A small inheritance arrives and he spends it in a single transaction: seven identical suits of dun velvet, one for each day of the week, bought together from the same tailor. He wears nothing else in public for the next ten years, and Paris gives him the name that outlasts every title he awards himself, the Velvet Gentleman. The uniform is a joke and it is also a solution. A man with seven identical suits never decides anything about clothes and never explains that he cannot buy new ones.
suggested_refs: The seven velvet suits of 1895, bought with a small inheritance

stops.name: Montmartre, the last room on the rue Cortot
stops.date_confidence: attested to the period 1896-1898; month unrecorded and defaulted
stops.campa: The money runs out. The room on the rue Cortot empties by degrees: he sells or pawns what furniture there is, plays cabaret for coins, and eats on the nights the cabaret pays. Biographers reckon these two years the poorest of his Montmartre life. In 1898 he gives up the Butte entirely and walks south out of Paris to a suburb where the rent is a fraction of this one. He is thirty-two, he has written the Gymnopédies and the Gnossiennes, and he cannot pay for a room on a hill.
suggested_refs: Satie's last Montmartre lodging, 6 rue Cortot, 1896-1898

segments.name: Arcueil, the House of Four Chimneys

stops.name: Arcueil, the single room at 22 rue Cauchy
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; month unrecorded and defaulted. The pool's geography lens placed the pin about 490 m north of the street; OpenStreetMap value used
stops.campa: He takes one room in a building called the Maison des Quatre Cheminées, at 22 rue Cauchy in Arcueil, a working suburb south of the city with a chemical works and a river. There is no running water and no electricity. He lives in this room for twenty-seven years and lets no one through the door in all that time, not Debussy, not Cocteau, not Milhaud, not the young composers who will name themselves after the suburb in his honour. What is inside is nobody's business until he is dead.
stops.quote: NOT being an orator, I cannot make a speech, I cannot even chat informally.
stops.quote_source: Erik Satie, 'A Learned Lecture on Music and Animals,' Vanity Fair, English translation, via Wikisource
suggested_refs: 22 rue Cauchy, Arcueil, the Maison des Quatre Cheminées

stops.name: Between Arcueil and Paris, the daily walk
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the daily walk recurs across the biographical tradition (Orledge, Volta) but the route and the stops are undocumented. Dated to the first full Arcueil year as a route marker, not a location
stops.campa: Almost every day for twenty-seven years he walks the ten kilometres into Paris and the ten kilometres back, in the velvet suit, carrying an umbrella, stopping at cafés along the way and writing in a notebook at the tables. The tradition holds that the pieces were composed on this road and copied out at night. The tradition also holds that he was drinking his way along it. Both can be true. The liver that fails in 1925 is the one carried up and down this road.
suggested_refs: The Arcueil to Paris walk, the cafés of the route unidentified
sources: Robert Orledge, Satie the Composer, and Ornella Volta, via the atlas geography lens (not independently documented)

stops.name: Paris, the cabaret songs
stops.date_confidence: representative midpoint of an attested period, c. 1898-1908; no single year applies
stops.campa: To pay for the room he writes and arranges some thirty songs for the cabaret singer Vincent Hyspa, topical numbers about the news of the week, and accompanies him on tour. In the same years come Je te veux, to a text by Henry Pacory, and La Diva de l'Empire, to one by Dominique Bonnaud and Numa Blès: a slow waltz and a music-hall march, both sold outright for whatever the publisher offered. The composer of Vexations is now a jobbing writer of tunes and says so without apology.
suggested_refs: The Hyspa settings, c. 1898-1908; 'Je te veux' (Pacory) and 'La Diva de l'Empire' (Bonnaud and Blès) are not Hyspa texts

stops.name: Paris, the premiere of Pelleas et Melisande
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; the pool gives no day, so the date is defaulted
stops.campa: He sits in the house for the first performance of Debussy's Pelléas et Mélisande and hears, done at full length with an orchestra, something he considers he sketched first and gave away. The opera is a triumph. Satie says nothing damaging in public, goes home to Arcueil and reconsiders what he is doing there. He is thirty-six, has no publisher and no standing. Three years later a man twice thrown out of the Conservatoire enrols as a student again.
suggested_refs: The 1902 premiere of Pelléas et Mélisande at the Opéra-Comique

stops.name: Paris, enrolling at the Schola Cantorum
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month
stops.campa: On the rue Saint-Jacques he presents himself at Vincent d'Indy's Schola Cantorum as a mature student and asks to be taught counterpoint. He is thirty-nine. He studies counterpoint with Albert Roussel and composition with d'Indy, submits exercises like a boy, and takes the discipline he refused at fifteen from teachers who represent everything he has spent twenty years mocking. His friends read it as a surrender. He calls it arming himself against the word primitive.
suggested_refs: The Schola Cantorum, rue Saint-Jacques, under Vincent d'Indy

stops.name: Paris, the counterpoint diploma
stops.date_confidence: diploma attested to 1908; the pool's geography lens calls 1908 the end of his studies while the chronology lens and en.wikipedia have him attending until 1912. Both dates stand, unreconciled in the sources
stops.campa: He is awarded a diploma in counterpoint and goes on attending classes until 1912. The paper is the only academic credential he ever holds, and he obtained it at forty-two by sitting exams beside students half his age. The music that follows the Schola is not more academic. It is drier and stranger than anything before it: preludes for a dog, dried embryos, and three pieces in the shape of a pear written to answer a critic who said his work had no form.
suggested_refs: Satie's 1908 Schola Cantorum diploma in counterpoint

stops.name: Paris, Ravel plays the second Sarabande
stops.date_confidence: attested to January 1911; the Salle Gaveau as venue is reconstruction, unverified in the sources the pool cites, and its coordinates are corrected from the lens value
stops.campa: At a concert of the Société musicale indépendante, Maurice Ravel plays the second Sarabande and other early pieces by a composer most of the audience believes to be dead or invented. The Sarabandes date from 1887, before Debussy had published anything. The harmonic language the room has been calling modern was set down by a cabaret pianist on the Butte twenty-four years earlier. Satie is forty-four, is famous for one evening, and will spend fourteen years being called the precursor.
suggested_refs: The Société musicale indépendante concert of January 1911; the venue attribution is unverified
sources: Robert Orledge, Satie the Composer, via the atlas geography lens (venue unverified)

stops.name: Arcueil, the flabby preludes for a dog
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; month unrecorded and defaulted
stops.campa: In the room at Arcueil he writes the Véritables Préludes flasques, pour un chien, the true flabby preludes for a dog, so titled because a critic had already complained about a set of flabby preludes he had not in fact written. The scores of this decade carry running commentary in the margins, addressed to the player and expressly forbidden to be read aloud to the audience. He is composing and annotating at once, and the annotations are the funnier half.
stops.quote: I love animals, and they return my affection. Animals know me, and they recognize me: especially dogs.
stops.quote_source: Erik Satie, 'A Learned Lecture on Music and Animals,' Vanity Fair, English translation, via Wikisource
suggested_refs: Véritables Préludes flasques (pour un chien), 1912

stops.name: Paris, Sports et divertissements
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; month unrecorded and defaulted
stops.campa: A publisher commissions twenty short pieces to sit beside Charles Martin's drawings of skating, golf, the tango and the corners of a picnic, and Satie writes them out in red ink in a calligraphic hand. The preface warns off the shrivelled and the dimwits, who are offered a ponderous chorale instead. Fritz Lang is on the butte of Montmartre this same year, painting. In August the war begins, and the album stays in the publisher's hands until long after it ends.
stops.quote: For the SHRIVELLED and the DIMWITS, I have written a suitably ponderous chorale ... I dedicate this chorale to those who do not like me.
stops.quote_source: Erik Satie, preface to Sports et divertissements (1914), in A Mammal's Notebook: Collected Writings of Erik Satie, ed. Ornella Volta, trans. Antony Melville (Atlas Press, 1996)
suggested_refs: Sports et divertissements, twenty pieces with Charles Martin's drawings, 1914

stops.name: Paris, meeting Jean Cocteau
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; the meeting place is unrecorded, so the pin is the Paris centroid
stops.campa: Jean Cocteau, twenty-six, restless and positioned everywhere at once, finds the Velvet Gentleman and decides that this is the composer for the ballet in his head. Cocteau has Diaghilev's ear. Seven years later he will send Man Ray to photograph Marcel Proust on his deathbed in the rue Hamelin; now he takes a fifty-year-old cabaret pianist out of Arcueil and puts him in front of the Ballets Russes. Satie, who has never written for an orchestra of that size, says yes.
suggested_refs: Jean Cocteau, scenarist of Parade and the link between Satie and Diaghilev

stops.name: Paris, composing Parade
stops.date_confidence: the composition period 1916-1917 is attested; the Polignac commission for Socrate is attested to October 1916, which fixes this stop's month
stops.campa: Through the war years he writes the score of Parade to Cocteau's scenario, with Picasso building cubist costumes a dancer can barely walk in and Massine making steps for them. Satie scores a typewriter, a steamship whistle, a pistol and a lottery wheel into the orchestra. In October the Princesse de Polignac commissions the separate work that becomes Socrate. In Zurich, at Hugo Ball's Cabaret Voltaire, Suzanne Perrottet is playing whole evenings of Satie to Dadaists who find him grotesque and keep listening.
stops.quote: People have always said to me: 'You will see when you're fifty (years of age)'. Well, I am fifty now, and I have seen nothing.
stops.quote_source: Attributed to Erik Satie; widely repeated but untraced beyond Wikiquote's 'source unknown' notation, and treated here as tradition rather than document
suggested_refs: The Polignac commission of October 1916; the Parade rehearsal studios are unrecorded

stops.name: Paris, Parade at the Theatre du Chatelet
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day, though the exact date comes from general Parade records rather than from the Satie chronology the pool fetched, which gives only the year
stops.campa: The Ballets Russes give Parade at the Châtelet: Cocteau's scenario, Picasso's curtain and costumes, Massine's choreography, Satie's typewriters. Part of the house howls. Guillaume Apollinaire, writing the programme note, reaches for a word that does not exist yet and calls the thing surréalisme. Six years earlier this same theatre held d'Annunzio's Martyre de Saint Sébastien, with Debussy's music and Bakst's décor. The hall is used to scandal. It has not heard a typewriter in the pit before.
suggested_refs: Picasso's Parade curtain, and Apollinaire's programme note coining surréalisme

stops.name: Paris, the postcard to Jean Poueigh
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the postcard follows Poueigh's hostile review, which fr.wikipedia places in May 1917. 30 May is the conventional date and no reachable source assigns a day
stops.campa: The critic Jean Poueigh shakes Satie's hand in the foyer and then prints a hostile review of Parade. Satie answers on an open postcard, sent through the post, where the concierge and anyone else along the way may read it. The card costs him a libel suit, a sentence and a fine. He is fifty-one, has just had the largest public success of his life, and throws a piece of it away rather than leave one sentence unwritten. The wording circulates in variants; every version ends with his signature.
stops.quote: Monsieur et cher ami – vous êtes un cul, un cul sans musique! Signé Erik Satie
stops.quote_source: Erik Satie, postcard to the critic Jean Poueigh, 1917, quoted in Wikipedia, 'Parade (ballet)', citing Mary Davis, Erik Satie, p. 120
suggested_refs: The Poueigh postcard, and the variant French reading 'vous n'etes qu'un cul, mais un cul sans musique'

stops.name: Paris, the libel trial
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1917; the month is unrecorded and defaulted, and the courtroom is inferred as the Paris courts of the period rather than documented
stops.campa: In court Cocteau shouts the offending word at Poueigh's lawyer and is taken outside and beaten by police for it. Satie is convicted, sentenced to eight days and fined; the Comtesse Étienne de Beaumont is said to have paid the money, and he does not go to prison. The affair does what the ballet alone could not and puts his name in newspapers that never review music. He is fifty-one and has a criminal conviction for calling a critic a name. He goes back to Arcueil, to the room nobody has entered, and begins setting Plato to music.
suggested_refs: The 1917 Poueigh libel proceedings; the courtroom is inferred, not documented
sources: Robert Orledge and Ornella Volta, via the atlas geography lens (venue inferred)

stops.name: Arcueil, finishing Socrate
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; month unrecorded and defaulted
stops.campa: For the Princesse de Polignac he sets the dialogues of Plato: the portrait of Socrates by Alcibiades, the walk beside the Ilissus, and the death, scored for four sopranos and a small orchestra in flat unornamented lines that refuse to react to anything they describe. The hemlock gets the same music as the riverbank. It is the least funny work he ever writes and the one he defends hardest against friends who wanted jokes. Debussy dies in March of this year, unreconciled with him.
suggested_refs: Socrate, symphonic drama on Victor Cousin's Plato translations, 1918

stops.name: Paris, the festival at the Salle Erard
stops.date_confidence: the 1920 festival is attested; the Salle Érard as venue is reconstruction, from concert-history references the pool did not re-fetch. Month unrecorded and defaulted
stops.campa: A festival of his music is given in Paris and the young come to it. He writes an Elégie among the Quatre petites mélodies and dedicates it to the memory of Debussy, two years after the quarrel and the death that closed it. Cocteau and Satie are by now called the spiritual fathers of Les Six, a group he did not form and does not lead, whose members treat the man of fifty-four in the worn velvet suit as the one figure in French music who never made a concession.
suggested_refs: The 1920 Satie festival; the Elégie of the Quatre petites mélodies, in memoriam Debussy

stops.name: Arcueil, the Ecole d'Arcueil
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; month unrecorded and defaulted
stops.campa: Four young composers, Henri Sauguet, Roger Désormière, Maxime Jacob and Henri Cliquet-Pleyel, name themselves the École d'Arcueil after the suburb, and come out to meet him at the café rather than the room, because nobody meets him in the room. In December of the same year, at the Théâtre des Champs-Élysées, Gurdjieff's pupils give their demonstrations of the sacred gymnastics in the hall of the Rite of Spring riot. Satie will open in that hall in twelve months.
suggested_refs: The École d'Arcueil: Sauguet, Désormière, Jacob, Cliquet-Pleyel

stops.name: Paris, Mercure and Relache
stops.date_confidence: the year is attested; the 4 December date and the Théâtre des Champs-Élysées as hall come from Orledge via the pool and were not independently re-fetched
stops.campa: In June, Massine and Picasso stage Mercure, poses plastiques to his music. In December the Ballets Suédois give Relâche, made with Francis Picabia, with René Clair's film Entr'acte running in the interval and Satie driven across the screen in a car. The curtain fails to rise on the first night, as advertised. In Monte Carlo, George Balanchine is arriving at the Ballets Russes to work with Stravinsky, Picasso and scores of Satie's. This is the last thing Satie stages.
stops.quote: The music for Relache? I was portraying people 'out on a spree'. Using popular themes for the purpose.
stops.quote_source: Erik Satie on his ballet Relache (1924), quoted in Wikipedia, 'Erik Satie'
suggested_refs: Relâche, Ballets Suédois, with René Clair's Entr'acte; Mercure, Massine and Picasso, June 1924
sources: Robert Orledge, Satie the Composer, via the atlas geography lens (date and venue not re-fetched)

stops.name: Paris, admitted to the Hopital Saint-Joseph
stops.date_confidence: attested to February 1925; the day is unrecorded and defaulted
stops.campa: The drinking of forty years presents its account. He is carried to the Hôpital Saint-Joseph on the rue Raymond-Losserand with cirrhosis and does not leave it again. Cocteau comes, Milhaud comes, the young men of Arcueil come; the Comte de Beaumont pays for the room. He is washed, fed and visited daily for five months, which is more attention than he has permitted anyone to give him since 1898. Picabia had set him down the year before, in the Relâche season, as a sad child sometimes made optimistic by alcohol.
stops.quote: He's a very susceptible man, arrogant, a real sad child, but one who is sometimes made optimistic by alcohol.
stops.quote_source: Francis Picabia on Erik Satie, quoted in Wikipedia, 'Erik Satie'
suggested_refs: Hopital Saint-Joseph, 185-189 rue Raymond-Losserand, Paris 14e

stops.name: Paris, death at the Hopital Saint-Joseph
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day
stops.campa: He dies on the first of July, fifty-nine years old, of a cirrhosis his friends afterwards describe as carefully cultivated. He leaves no wife, no children, no debts anyone can find and no address book. The last months are spent among visitors he has known for thirty years and never once invited home. Nobody in the room has any idea what is in the room at Arcueil, and the key is in his coat. The white foods he claimed to live on were a joke he printed. The drinking was not.
stops.quote: I eat only white foods: eggs, sugar, grated bones, the fat of dead animals; veal, salt, coconut, chicken cooked in white water; fruit mold, rice, turnips; camphorated sausage, dough, cheese (white), cotton salad, and certain fish (skinless).
stops.quote_source: Erik Satie, quoted in Rollo H. Myers, Erik Satie (Dover, 1968), p. 135
suggested_refs: The death certificate of 1 July 1925, Hopital Saint-Joseph, Paris

stops.name: Arcueil, the room opened
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: a much-retold anecdote whose details vary between accounts, tagged [A] by two of the pool's lenses and [R] by a third. July 1925, exact day unrecorded and defaulted
stops.campa: His brother Conrad and his friends unlock the door at 22 rue Cauchy and walk into a room no visitor has entered in twenty-seven years. The accounts differ in every detail and agree on the shape: two ruined pianos, one on the other or tied together, the pedals bound with string; letters in heaps, many of them unopened; umbrellas by the dozen; false collars; a wardrobe of identical grey velvet suits worn to the weave; and behind the pianos, scores nobody knew existed, an opera among them.
suggested_refs: The Arcueil room inventory of July 1925, as recounted by Conrad Satie, Milhaud and Cocteau
sources: Ornella Volta and Robert Orledge, via the atlas geography lens (details vary between accounts)

stops.name: Arcueil, buried in the cemetery of the suburb
stops.date_confidence: attested to July 1925; the day is unrecorded and defaulted within the month. Three different coordinate pairs appear across the pool's lenses (48.8065/2.3312, 48.8025/2.3339, OpenStreetMap 48.8040/2.3402); the OpenStreetMap pair is used
stops.campa: They bury him in the cemetery at Arcueil, in the suburb, not on the hill in Paris where the artists lie. The grave takes a plain white cross. From here it is ten kilometres to the Butte he walked out of in 1898 and ten kilometres back, the distance he covered on foot almost every day of the twenty-seven years between. Sauguet and the others of the École d'Arcueil follow the coffin out. Four towns will put his name on their streets before the century ends.
suggested_refs: Satie's grave with its white cross, Cimetiere d'Arcueil

stops.name: New York, Cage plays Vexations through
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day
stops.campa: At the Pocket Theatre on Third Avenue, John Cage takes the seventy-year-old marginal note literally and mounts the first complete Vexations: eight hundred and forty repetitions in a relay of pianists, more than eighteen hours, with David Tudor, Christian Wolff, John Cale and Joshua Rifkin among them. Admission is five dollars with five cents refunded for every twenty minutes endured, an arithmetic Cage has not worked out. Fifteen years earlier he had put Buckminster Fuller on stage at Black Mountain College as the Baron Medusa in a Satie play.
suggested_refs: The Pocket Theatre relay of 9 September 1963, and Cage's 1948 Black Mountain staging of Le Piege de Meduse

stops.name: Honfleur, the house opens as Les Maisons Satie
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day
stops.campa: On the Fête de la Musique the three linked half-timbered houses where he was born open as a museum. The façades have been listed since 1992. Inside there is no glass case: a self-playing grand, a mechanical winged pear with wings that beat, the umbrellas, the false collars, and the room staged as the friends found it in 1925. The town that produced a boy who let nobody into his room has turned the room into an exhibit and takes money at the door.
suggested_refs: Les Maisons Satie, 67 boulevard Charles V, Honfleur, opened 21 June 1998
